prompt: What is the most reliable immediate indicator that bag-valve-mask ventilations are effective?

options.text: Visible chest rise with each ventilation
A pulse oximeter reading that rises within seconds
Resistance felt in the bag as each breath is squeezed
Abdomen rising and falling with each ventilation

explanation: Visible chest rise with each squeeze is the immediate sign of an adequate tidal volume. SpO2 changes lag behind, rising bag resistance suggests a problem, and abdominal rise means air is going to the stomach.

distractorExplanations.b: SpO2 lags behind ventilation by a minute or more and can mislead with poor perfusion or CO; chest rise is the immediate sign.
distractorExplanations.c: Rising bag resistance suggests airway obstruction, gastric distension, or poor lung compliance, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach (gastric insufflation) from excess volume or poor head position.

prompt: An adult patient with suspected opioid overdose is unresponsive with slow, shallow respirations. After scene safety and airway opening, the priority intervention is

options.text: Place in the recovery position and observe breathing closely
Support ventilation with BVM/oxygen and consider naloxone
Give naloxone and wait for breathing to improve on its own
Apply a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min and monitor

explanation: Opioid overdose kills by respiratory depression. The EMT opens the airway and assists ventilation with a BVM and oxygen first, then gives naloxone per protocol; ventilation continues until breathing is adequate.

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position protects the airway but does not fix slow, shallow breathing; ventilations must be assisted.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone takes minutes to act; inadequate ventilation is supported with a BVM first rather than waiting.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather requires adequate spontaneous breathing; slow, shallow respirations need assisted BVM ventilation.

prompt: A patient with a suspected pulmonary embolism is alert and breathing adequately at 24 per minute, but SpO2 is 85%. Which device delivers the highest oxygen concentration?

options.text: Nasal cannula at 6 L/min, its upper limit
Simple face mask at 8 L/min with humidity
Nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Venturi mask set to deliver 28% oxygen

explanation: A nonrebreather with the reservoir bag inflated, at 10–15 L/min, delivers the highest concentration (about 60–90%) to a patient who is breathing adequately. Nasal cannulas and simple masks deliver much less; a Venturi mask is for precise low concentrations.

distractorExplanations.a: A nasal cannula tops out around 40–44% oxygen, far less than a nonrebreather.
distractorExplanations.b: A simple mask delivers roughly 40–60%; a nonrebreather with a full reservoir reaches about 90%.
distractorExplanations.d: A Venturi mask gives precise low concentrations for titration, not maximum oxygen.

prompt: Stridor in an upper-airway obstruction patient suggests

options.text: Bronchoconstriction of the lower airways
Fluid in the alveoli from acute pulmonary edema
Complete obstruction with no air movement
Partial obstruction at or above the larynx

explanation: Stridor is a hallmark of upper airway narrowing and is an emergency warning sign. It produces a high-pitched inspiratory sound.

distractorExplanations.a: Lower-airway narrowing produces expiratory wheezing, not the inspiratory stridor of an upper airway obstruction.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales), not the high-pitched inspiratory sound of stridor.
distractorExplanations.c: Complete obstruction is silent; stridor requires air moving past a partial narrowing.

prompt: An unresponsive adult with no gag reflex needs an oropharyngeal airway. How is the correct OPA size measured?

options.text: From the corner of the mouth to the earlobe
From the tip of the nose to the earlobe
From the chin to the sternal notch
By the width of the patient's little finger

explanation: An OPA is measured from the corner of the mouth to the earlobe (or angle of the jaw) and used only in unresponsive patients without a gag reflex. Too long pushes the epiglottis down; too short pushes the tongue back into the airway.

distractorExplanations.b: That is the nasopharyngeal airway measurement, not the OPA.
distractorExplanations.c: Neck length does not predict OPA size.
distractorExplanations.d: Little-finger width is an old estimate for NPA diameter, not OPA length.

prompt: The head-tilt/chin-lift is generally avoided in trauma patients because

options.text: It pushes the tongue back into the airway
It may worsen cervical spine injury
It raises intracranial pressure in head injuries
It is less effective than the jaw-thrust

explanation: The head-tilt/chin-lift extends the neck and can worsen a cervical spine injury, so trauma patients get a jaw-thrust with manual stabilization instead.

distractorExplanations.a: The maneuver lifts the tongue off the pharynx; the trauma concern is neck extension worsening a spinal injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Airway positioning does not meaningfully raise ICP; the concern is spinal movement from neck extension.
distractorExplanations.d: The head-tilt/chin-lift is usually the more effective maneuver; it is avoided in trauma because of neck extension, not efficacy.

prompt: Wheezing is most commonly associated with:

options.text: Upper airway swelling at the larynx
Fluid in the alveoli of the lungs
Lower airway bronchoconstriction
Collapse of a lung from pneumothorax

explanation: Expiratory wheeze reflects narrowed lower airways; still assess for other causes. Asthma and COPD exacerbations are the classic causes.

distractorExplanations.a: Laryngeal swelling causes high-pitched inspiratory stridor, not the expiratory wheezing of narrowed bronchioles.
distractorExplanations.b: Alveolar fluid produces crackles (rales); wheezing comes from narrowed lower airways.
distractorExplanations.d: Pneumothorax causes diminished or absent breath sounds on the affected side, not wheezing.

prompt: A patient with inadequate breathing should receive

options.text: High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather at 15 L/min
CPAP at low pressure to improve oxygenation and lung expansion
A nasopharyngeal airway with blow-by oxygen
Assisted positive-pressure ventilation (e.g., BVM)

explanation: Inadequate rate or depth means the patient is not moving enough air. Oxygen alone does not ventilate; assisted positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM and supplemental oxygen is required.

distractorExplanations.a: A nonrebreather adds oxygen but does not move air; inadequate rate or depth requires assisted ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: CPAP needs an alert patient who breathes adequately on their own; inadequate breathing calls for BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: An NPA keeps the airway open but does not ventilate, and blow-by oxygen cannot correct poor ventilation.

prompt: CPAP in EMS (when indicated and available) primarily helps patients with:

options.text: Respiratory distress from conditions like CHF/pulmonary edema
Respiratory distress from a suspected tension pneumothorax
Inadequate breathing with a decreased level of responsiveness
Respiratory distress with systolic BP below 90 mm Hg

explanation: CPAP requires a spontaneously breathing cooperative patient; not for arrest or complete obstruction. It stents the airways open and improves oxygenation.

distractorExplanations.b: Positive pressure can enlarge a pneumothorax; suspected pneumothorax is a CPAP contraindication.
distractorExplanations.c: CPAP needs an alert patient who protects their airway and breathes adequately; this patient needs BVM ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Hypotension is a CPAP contraindication because positive pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output.

prompt: Cyanosis indicates

options.text: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Significant hypoxemia
Severe anemia with normal SpO2
Peripheral vasodilation

explanation: Central cyanosis is a late, serious sign of poor oxygenation. It calls for urgent airway, oxygen, and ventilation assessment.

distractorExplanations.a: CO poisoning typically does not cause cyanosis; skin color and pulse oximetry can look falsely normal.
distractorExplanations.c: Anemia causes pallor; cyanosis needs enough deoxygenated hemoglobin, which anemic patients may lack.
distractorExplanations.d: Vasodilation causes flushed, red skin; the bluish color of cyanosis reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin.

prompt: A patient with severe asthma is wheezing less than before and becoming drowsy with poor air movement. This most likely indicates

options.text: The attack is resolving as the bronchospasm eases
Drowsiness as an expected side effect of nebulized albuterol
Worsening obstruction and impending respiratory failure
Hyperventilation from anxiety lowering CO2 levels

explanation: Silent chest/fatigue with drowsiness signals exhaustion and failure—support ventilation and ALS.

distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with drowsiness and poor air movement means too little airflow to wheeze — a silent chest, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.b: Albuterol causes tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety, not sedation; drowsiness here signals exhaustion.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation causes rapid breathing and tingling, not drowsiness with poor air movement.

prompt: The preferred method to open the airway of a trauma patient with possible c-spine injury is

options.text: Head-tilt/chin-lift once a rigid cervical collar is applied
Sniffing position with the head slightly extended back
Jaw-thrust after log-rolling the patient onto one side
Jaw-thrust while maintaining manual cervical stabilization

explanation: The jaw-thrust opens the airway by lifting the mandible without extending the neck, so it is the preferred maneuver while another rescuer holds manual cervical stabilization.

distractorExplanations.a: A collar does not prevent the extension of a head-tilt; jaw-thrust with manual stabilization is used instead.
distractorExplanations.b: The sniffing position extends the neck; it is for non-trauma airway positioning, not suspected c-spine injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Rolling before manual stabilization moves the spine; the jaw-thrust is done with the head held inline in the position found.

prompt: Adequate adult ventilation rate with a BVM for a patient with a pulse (general guideline concept) is approximately

options.text: About 1 breath every 5–6 seconds (roughly 10–12/min)
As fast as possible until the SpO2 reaches 100%
About 1 breath every 10–12 seconds (roughly 5–6/min)
30 compressions to 2 breaths, as in adult CPR

explanation: Avoid hyperventilation; deliver breaths that produce chest rise at an appropriate rate. Each breath should be just enough to produce visible chest rise.

distractorExplanations.b: Rapid ventilation causes hyperventilation, gastric inflation, and reduced venous return; aim for 10–12 per minute.
distractorExplanations.c: Five to six breaths per minute under-ventilates an adult with a pulse; deliver one breath every 5–6 seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: 30:2 is the CPR ratio for a pulseless patient; a patient with a pulse receives rescue breaths without compressions.

prompt: Suctioning an adult patient's airway should be limited to approximately

options.text: No more than about 5 seconds per adult attempt
No more than about 15 seconds per attempt
No more than about 30 seconds per attempt
One attempt, then switch to finger sweeps

explanation: Brief suction clears the airway; prolonged suction worsens hypoxia—reoxygenate between attempts. Monitor oxygenation during and between attempts.

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is the infant limit; adults can be suctioned for up to about 15 seconds per attempt.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty seconds doubles the adult limit and causes hypoxia and vagal bradycardia.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeated brief suction passes with reoxygenation are acceptable; blind finger sweeps can push material deeper.

prompt: A nonrebreather mask is most appropriate when:

options.text: The patient is apneic and needs artificial ventilation
A COPD patient needs precise low-flow oxygen titration
A breathing patient needs high-concentration oxygen
A stable patient with SpO2 of 93% needs mild supplementation

explanation: NRB delivers high FiO2 to spontaneously breathing patients; apneic patients need BVM/advanced airway support. The patient must also be able to tolerate the mask.

distractorExplanations.a: Apnea requires positive-pressure ventilation.
distractorExplanations.b: Precise FiO2 titration is the job of a Venturi mask; a nonrebreather delivers high, non-adjustable concentrations.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild hypoxemia in a stable patient is usually titrated with a nasal cannula toward 94%; the NRB is for high-concentration needs.

prompt: For an unresponsive adult with no normal breathing and no pulse, the immediate action is

options.text: Begin high-quality CPR and apply AED as soon as available
Give 2 rescue breaths and recheck the pulse for 1 minute
Give rescue breaths at 1 every 6 seconds without compressions
Check blood glucose before starting compressions

explanation: For an unresponsive adult with no normal breathing and no pulse, start high-quality compressions immediately and attach the AED as soon as it arrives. Every minute without CPR and defibrillation lowers survival.

distractorExplanations.b: Compressions start immediately (C-A-B), and pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds in a suspected arrest.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient with a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: Reversible causes such as hypoglycemia are considered after compressions and defibrillation are underway.

prompt: High-quality adult CPR compression depth is approximately

options.text: About 1.5 inches (4 cm)
At least 2 inches (5 cm)
At least 3 inches (7.5 cm)
One-half of the chest's depth

explanation: AHA-aligned adult depth is at least 2 inches with full recoil and adequate rate. Allow full chest recoil after each compression.

distractorExplanations.a: About 1.5 inches is the infant compression depth; adults need at least 2 inches (5 cm).
distractorExplanations.c: Depths beyond about 2.4 inches (6 cm) increase injury risk without benefit; the adult target is 2–2.4 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: Half the AP depth is far too deep; adults need 2–2.4 inches, and children about one-third of the AP depth.

prompt: An AED advises a shock. You should

options.text: Check a carotid pulse for 10 seconds before shocking
Resume CPR for 2 minutes, then shock at the next analysis
Ensure no one is touching the patient, deliver the shock
Keep compressing while the AED delivers the shock

explanation: When the AED advises a shock, clear everyone from the patient, press shock, then resume compressions immediately without a pulse check.

distractorExplanations.a: A pulse check delays defibrillation; once the AED advises a shock, clear the patient and shock without a pulse check.
distractorExplanations.b: An advised shock is delivered now; delaying it lowers the chance of converting VF or pulseless VT.
distractorExplanations.d: Touching the patient during the shock risks injuring the rescuer; everyone is cleared before shocking.

prompt: Aspirin is given in suspected ACS (per protocol) primarily because it

options.text: Dissolves existing coronary clots like a fibrinolytic in the field
Dilates coronary arteries to relieve the chest pain
Relieves cardiac pain as an analgesic at this low dose
Inhibits platelet aggregation and may limit clot progression

explanation: Aspirin blocks platelet aggregation, limiting growth of the clot in the coronary artery. EMTs give 162–324 mg chewed per protocol unless the patient is allergic or has another contraindication.

distractorExplanations.a: Aspirin does not lyse formed clots; fibrinolytic drugs do that in the hospital.
distractorExplanations.b: Coronary vasodilation is the action of nitroglycerin; aspirin is given as an antiplatelet agent.
distractorExplanations.c: Low-dose (162–324 mg) aspirin is given for its antiplatelet effect, not analgesia; pain relief comes from nitro or opioids.

prompt: Nitroglycerin is contraindicated when:

options.text: The patient has used a PDE-5 inhibitor recently or has hypotension
The patient has chest pain that started more than 12 hours ago
The patient's systolic blood pressure is 150 mm Hg with a headache
The patient already chewed 324 mg of aspirin for this episode

explanation: Nitroglycerin dilates blood vessels and can cause profound hypotension. It is withheld when systolic BP is below the protocol cutoff (about 90–100 mm Hg) or after recent PDE-5 inhibitor use such as sildenafil or tadalafil.

distractorExplanations.b: Symptom duration does not contraindicate nitroglycerin; contraindications are low BP and recent PDE-5 inhibitor use.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic of 150 is above the hypotension cutoff (about 90–100 mm Hg); headache is a common side effect, not a contraindication.
distractorExplanations.d: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are given together in suspected ACS; prior aspirin is not a contraindication.

prompt: Right-sided heart failure commonly presents with:

options.text: Crackles in both lungs and pink, frothy sputum
Peripheral edema and JVD from systemic congestion
Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Unilateral calf swelling with warmth and tenderness

explanation: Right-sided failure backs up into the systemic veins; left-sided often causes pulmonary edema.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulmonary edema signs reflect left-sided failure backing up into the lungs, not systemic congestion.
distractorExplanations.c: Orthopnea and PND come from pulmonary congestion in left-sided heart failure.
distractorExplanations.d: One swollen, tender calf suggests deep vein thrombosis, not the bilateral edema of right heart failure.

prompt: Two EMTs are performing CPR on an adult who has no advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?

options.text: Continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds

explanation: Adult CPR without an advanced airway uses 30 compressions to 2 breaths for one or two rescuers. After an advanced airway is placed, compressions are continuous with 1 breath every 6 seconds. 15:2 applies to two-rescuer child and infant CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: 5:1 is an outdated ratio removed from AHA guidelines long ago.
distractorExplanations.b: 15:2 is the two-rescuer ratio for children and infants, not adults.
distractorExplanations.d: Asynchronous breaths every 6 seconds are used only after an advanced airway is placed.

prompt: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is suggested by:

options.text: Asystole on the monitor after two minutes of CPR
A sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 readings
Fixed, dilated pupils after resuscitation
Return of organized pulse after arrest care

explanation: ROSC is the return of a palpable pulse and blood pressure, often with an abrupt rise in ETCO2 and the patient breathing or moving. Post-arrest care focuses on ventilation, oxygenation and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Asystole is a flat line with no electrical activity, the opposite of returning circulation.
distractorExplanations.b: ROSC typically causes an abrupt rise in ETCO2; a drop suggests poor perfusion or a displaced airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Fixed, dilated pupils indicate poor cerebral perfusion and do not signal returning circulation.

prompt: Chest pain described as pressure with radiation to the arm/jaw in an adult should be treated as:

options.text: Possible acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise
Musculoskeletal strain unless the ECG is abnormal
A panic attack if the patient is young and anxious
Acid reflux if the pain began within an hour after a large meal

explanation: Pressure-like chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw is a classic acute coronary syndrome presentation. EMTs treat it as cardiac until a hospital rules it out: oxygen if hypoxic, aspirin and nitroglycerin per protocol, a 12-lead if available, and prompt transport.

distractorExplanations.b: A normal or unavailable ECG does not exclude ACS; classic radiating pressure is treated as cardiac.
distractorExplanations.c: Anxiety can coexist with ACS; radiating pressure must be managed as cardiac until ruled out.
distractorExplanations.d: Meal timing does not rule out ACS; GI causes are diagnoses of exclusion made in the hospital.

prompt: Automated external defibrillation is indicated for:

options.text: Ventricular tachycardia in an alert patient with a strong pulse
Pulseless ventricular fibrillation / ventricular tachycardia
Pulseless electrical activity and asystole on the monitor
Unresponsive patients with a slow pulse and poor perfusion

explanation: AEDs analyze the rhythm and shock only ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Patients with a pulse are never shocked, and PEA and asystole are treated with CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: VT with a pulse is not an AED indication; AEDs are applied only to unresponsive, pulseless patients.
distractorExplanations.c: PEA and asystole are non-shockable rhythms; they are treated with CPR, not defibrillation.
distractorExplanations.d: Symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse is not shockable; it needs ventilation support and ALS, not defibrillation.

prompt: An adult collapses at a gym. She is unresponsive with occasional gasping breaths, and no pulse is felt within 10 seconds. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Apply a nonrebreather, since she is still breathing
Place her in the recovery position and monitor
Treat it as cardiac arrest and start CPR
Assist ventilations only, without compressions

explanation: Occasional gasping (agonal breathing) is common in the first minutes of cardiac arrest and is not normal breathing. An unresponsive patient with only gasps and no definite pulse gets immediate CPR and an AED.

distractorExplanations.a: Agonal gasps are not effective breathing; this is cardiac arrest.
distractorExplanations.b: The recovery position is for adequate breathing with a pulse; gasping without a pulse is arrest.
distractorExplanations.d: Without a pulse, ventilation alone cannot circulate blood; compressions are required.

Reanalyze the rhythm right away to confirm the shock worked
Remove the pads and begin rescue breathing only
Resume CPR immediately for about 2 minutes, then reanalyze

prompt: A patient with chest pain took one of her prescribed nitroglycerin tablets 5 minutes ago with no relief. BP is 136/84, and medical direction approves another dose. What is typical?

options.text: One 0.4 mg tablet under the tongue, then recheck BP
Two tablets at once to make up for the poor response
One tablet swallowed with water for a longer effect
Wait 30 minutes before any further dose

explanation: Assisted nitroglycerin is typically one 0.4 mg sublingual tablet or spray every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses total, if systolic BP stays above about 100 mm Hg (per protocol) and no PDE-5 inhibitor was taken. BP and pain are reassessed after each dose.

distractorExplanations.b: Doses are given one at a time, about 5 minutes apart, with BP rechecked.
distractorExplanations.c: Swallowed nitroglycerin is largely broken down by the liver; it is given sublingually.
distractorExplanations.d: Repeat doses are typically every 5 minutes, up to 3 total, per protocol.

prompt: A 78-year-old is dizzy and pale with a pulse of 38 and BP 78/46. She is alert and breathing adequately. What should the EMT prioritize?

options.text: Start chest compressions because the pulse is under 40
Support ABCs, request ALS, and transport promptly
Apply AED pads and shock to reset the rhythm
Give aspirin and nitroglycerin for possible ACS

explanation: Symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension is a perfusion problem. EMTs support airway and breathing, give oxygen if hypoxic, keep the patient supine, request ALS for pacing or drugs and transport promptly. Compressions and AED shocks are not for an adult who has a pulse.

distractorExplanations.a: An adult with a palpable pulse does not get compressions; the problem is slow perfusion.
distractorExplanations.c: AEDs shock only pulseless VF or VT; a patient with a pulse is never shocked.
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin with a systolic BP of 78 can worsen shock; hypotension is a contraindication.

prompt: A patient with a VAD (ventricular assist device) is unresponsive and pulseless by usual means. The EMT should

options.text: Assume death because no pulse is palpable
Place AED pads directly over the device driveline
Follow local VAD/cardiac arrest protocols
Disconnect the device power to reset its alarms

explanation: VAD patients need specialized protocols; lack of palpable pulse may be expected—use device assessment cues and local rules. This often means CPR if indicated and contacting medical direction or the device coordinator.

distractorExplanations.a: Continuous-flow VADs often produce no palpable pulse; absence of a pulse alone does not confirm arrest or death.
distractorExplanations.b: Pads are placed away from the device and driveline; placing them over hardware can damage the pump.
distractorExplanations.d: Disconnecting power stops the pump; controllers stay connected and troubleshooting follows the VAD team's guidance.

prompt: The primary survey in trauma follows which priority concept?

options.text: Find and fix life threats first
Complete a SAMPLE history before any exam
Splint long-bone fractures before moving on
Transport only after full secondary survey

explanation: The primary survey finds and treats immediate life threats in order (massive bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation) before any detailed history or secondary exam. Critical patients are packaged for rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.b: SAMPLE history belongs to the secondary assessment, after immediate life threats are addressed.
distractorExplanations.c: Splinting is part of secondary care; airway, breathing, and bleeding control come first.
distractorExplanations.d: Critical patients are transported early; the full secondary survey may happen en route or not at all.

prompt: A sucking chest wound (open pneumothorax) is initially managed by:

options.text: Bulky gauze dressing packed into the wound
Occlusive dressing sealed on three sides
Pressure dressing wrapped tightly around the chest
Needle decompression of the chest by the EMT

explanation: Three-sided occlusive dressing can prevent air entry while allowing escape; monitor for tension. A commercial vented chest seal may be used per protocol.

distractorExplanations.c: A tight circumferential wrap restricts chest expansion and does not seal the wound against air entry.
distractorExplanations.d: Needle decompression is beyond EMT scope and treats tension pneumothorax, not initial open-wound care.

prompt: External arterial bleeding that is life-threatening should be controlled by:

options.text: Elevation and pressure-point compression
A loose dressing with the patient in shock position
Direct pressure and tourniquet use when indicated
Tourniquet only after 10 minutes of failed pressure

explanation: Life-threatening extremity bleeding is controlled with firm direct pressure and, if that fails or the bleeding is clearly massive, a tourniquet placed high and tight. Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended.

distractorExplanations.a: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for life-threatening bleeding; use pressure, then a tourniquet.
distractorExplanations.b: A loose dressing does not stop arterial flow, and Trendelenburg positioning is not a hemorrhage control method.
distractorExplanations.d: Delaying a tourniquet for a fixed time wastes blood; apply it as soon as pressure fails or bleeding is clearly massive.

prompt: After a steering-wheel impact, a section of a driver's right chest wall moves inward when he inhales and outward when he exhales. What does this suggest?

options.text: Simple pneumothorax
Rib contusion without fracture
Cardiac tamponade
Flail chest

explanation: Paradoxical movement of a chest segment means two or more adjacent ribs are fractured in two or more places (flail chest). It impairs ventilation and often hides a lung contusion; EMTs assist ventilation with a BVM as needed and stabilize the segment per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: A simple pneumothorax reduces breath sounds but does not make a chest segment move opposite the rest of the wall.
distractorExplanations.b: A bruised rib hurts but cannot move on its own; paradoxical motion needs ribs broken in two or more places.
distractorExplanations.c: Tamponade causes JVD, hypotension and muffled heart tones, not paradoxical chest wall motion.

prompt: For a suspected pelvic fracture with shock, EMS should

options.text: Stabilize pelvis per protocol and treat for shock
Compress and rock the iliac crests to confirm instability
Apply a traction splint to the leg on the injured side
Elevate the legs in shock position before stabilizing

explanation: Pelvic fractures can cause massive bleeding; minimize movement and stabilize. Avoid excessive log-rolling.

distractorExplanations.b: Repeated rocking or springing of the pelvis can dislodge clots and worsen bleeding; it is not used to confirm a fracture.
distractorExplanations.c: Traction splints are contraindicated with pelvic fractures because the device pushes against the ischium and pelvis.
distractorExplanations.d: Raising the legs moves the fractured pelvis and delays stabilization; immobilize the pelvis first and limit movement.

prompt: On a July afternoon, a roofer is confused and combative, with hot skin and a temperature of 105.4°F (40.8°C). What is the priority?

Treat as heat exhaustion: rest in the shade only
Rapid active cooling and prompt transport

explanation: Heat stroke is a core temperature above about 104°F (40°C) with altered mental status. distractorExplanations.b: Covering traps heat; heat stroke needs aggressive cooling.

Into the deltoid muscle of the upper arm
Into the upper outer buttock muscle
Under the skin beside the navel

distractorExplanations.b: Auto-injectors are designed and labeled for the thigh; the deltoid gives less reliable absorption.
distractorExplanations.c: The buttock risks injection into fat or near the sciatic nerve; the labeled site is the outer thigh.
distractorExplanations.d: Abdominal subcutaneous injection is for insulin and heparin, not intramuscular epinephrine.

Suction of the mouth with a rigid catheter
A nasopharyngeal airway

distractorExplanations.b: BVM ventilation is appropriate if breathing becomes inadequate.
distractorExplanations.c: Oral suction is safe and often needed to clear blood or vomit.

prompt: How should an EMT position an unresponsive infant's head to open the airway?

options.text: Neutral position with a pad under the shoulders
Chin flexed down onto the chest for protection
Hyperextended as far back as the neck allows
Turned fully to one side with a pillow under the head

explanation: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when lying flat. A thin pad under the shoulders brings the head to a neutral (sniffing) position, which opens the airway without kinking the soft trachea.

distractorExplanations.b: Flexing the neck pushes the tongue back and blocks the airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Hyperextension kinks the soft infant trachea and can close the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: A pillow flexes the neck; infants need padding under the shoulders, not the head.

prompt: A COPD patient is in respiratory distress with SpO2 84% on room air. What should the EMT do about oxygen?

options.text: Withhold oxygen because it will stop her drive to breathe
Give 15 L/min by nonrebreather and never reduce it
Give oxygen and titrate to the protocol target
Give oxygen only if the SpO2 drops below 70%

explanation: Hypoxic COPD patients need oxygen. EMTs give it and titrate to the protocol target (often 88–92% for known CO2 retainers), watching mental status and breathing; if breathing becomes inadequate, they assist with a BVM.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypoxia is far more dangerous; oxygen is given and titrated, not withheld.
distractorExplanations.b: COPD patients are titrated to a target saturation, often 88–92%, rather than maximal oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for severe hypoxemia risks cardiac arrhythmias and arrest.

prompt: A family is found drowsy in a house with a running generator. One patient's SpO2 reads 99%. How should the EMT interpret this reading?

options.text: It means oxygen therapy would be harmful here
It proves the patient's blood oxygen is fine
It shows the generator exhaust was not the cause
It may be falsely normal from carbon monoxide

explanation: Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated hemoglobin, so SpO2 can look normal in carbon monoxide poisoning. EMTs remove patients from the source, give high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather and transport, using a CO-oximeter if available.

distractorExplanations.a: High-flow oxygen is the treatment for CO poisoning.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulse oximeters cannot tell carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin.
distractorExplanations.c: SpO2 does not measure CO exposure; symptoms and scene suggest it.

prompt: An alert asthmatic is wheezing and has her own prescribed albuterol inhaler. What must be true before the EMT assists her with it?

Her SpO2 is below 85% on room air
She has used it at least twice in the past hour
A family member requests that it be given

explanation: EMTs may assist with a patient's own prescribed metered-dose inhaler when the patient has signs of bronchospasm, is alert enough to use it, the device is theirs and unexpired, and protocol or medical direction allows it. The maximum number of doses is noted.

distractorExplanations.b: Assisting does not require severe hypoxemia; it treats bronchospasm.
distractorExplanations.c: Recent use is noted, but it is not what authorizes the assist.
distractorExplanations.d: Family requests do not authorize medication administration.

prompt: Five minutes after assisted albuterol, a patient's heart rate rises from 100 to 118 and her hands are shaky. Her breathing is easier. What does this most likely mean?

options.text: A heart attack triggered by the inhaler
Worsening asthma with impending respiratory failure
An allergic reaction requiring epinephrine
Expected side effects of albuterol

explanation: Albuterol is a beta-2 agonist that relaxes bronchial smooth muscle but also commonly causes tachycardia, tremor and nervousness. These expected effects are monitored and reported; improved breathing shows the drug is working.

distractorExplanations.a: A modest rate rise with tremor is a typical beta-agonist effect, not ACS.
distractorExplanations.b: Her breathing is easier; failure shows exhaustion and drowsiness.
distractorExplanations.c: Tremor and tachycardia without hives or hypotension are not anaphylaxis.

prompt: A patient who breathes through a permanent tracheal stoma has inadequate respirations. How should the EMT ventilate?

options.text: Mouth-to-mouth after covering the stoma with a hand
BVM with an infant or child mask over the stoma
Nonrebreather mask over the face at 15 L/min
BVM sealed over the mouth and nose as usual

explanation: In a neck breather, ventilate directly through the stoma: a small round infant or child mask seals well over it. If air escapes from the mouth and nose, close them. Suction the stoma as needed.

distractorExplanations.a: This still sends air the wrong way and skips the oxygen-enriched BVM.
distractorExplanations.c: A nonrebreather does not ventilate, and it is over the wrong opening.
distractorExplanations.d: Air from the mouth cannot reach the lungs when the trachea opens at the neck.

prompt: During BVM ventilation, the patient's abdomen is becoming distended. What should the EMT adjust first?

options.text: Faster breaths to push air past the obstruction
Smaller, slower breaths with good head position
Press hard on the abdomen to empty the stomach
Larger breaths to overcome the abdominal pressure

explanation: Gastric distension comes from excessive volume or pressure. Reposition the airway, deliver just enough volume for visible chest rise over about 1 second, and slow the rate. Have suction ready because distension raises vomiting risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Faster, forceful breaths send more air into the stomach.
distractorExplanations.c: Abdominal pressure can cause vomiting and aspiration.
distractorExplanations.d: Bigger volumes worsen gastric inflation and vomiting risk.

prompt: A 4-year-old is sitting upright leaning forward, drooling, with a high fever and soft stridor. What should the EMT avoid?

options.text: Letting the child stay in the parent's lap
Looking in the throat with a tongue depressor
Transporting promptly while keeping the child calm
Offering blow-by oxygen held by the parent

explanation: Drooling, tripod positioning, high fever and stridor suggest epiglottitis. Agitating the child or inspecting the throat can trigger complete airway obstruction. Keep the child calm in a position of comfort, give blow-by oxygen and transport promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: A calm position of comfort on the parent's lap is encouraged.
distractorExplanations.c: Prompt, calm transport is the right plan.
distractorExplanations.d: Gentle blow-by oxygen without upsetting the child is appropriate.

prompt: A young adult is breathing 32 per minute after an argument, with tingling fingers. Which statement about her care is correct?

options.text: Rule out medical causes; never use a paper bag
Withhold oxygen because anxiety is the only cause
Tell her to hold her breath until the tingling stops
Have her rebreathe into a paper bag to raise CO2

explanation: Rapid breathing with tingling can come from anxiety, but also from hypoxia, pulmonary embolism, DKA or poisoning. EMTs assess fully, coach slower breathing, give oxygen if hypoxic and never use a paper bag.

distractorExplanations.b: Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion; hypoxia must be ruled out.
distractorExplanations.c: Breath-holding is not a treatment and ignores possible medical causes.
distractorExplanations.d: Paper bags can cause hypoxia and miss serious causes such as PE or DKA.

prompt: A 2-year-old with severe respiratory distress becomes listless, and her heart rate drops from 170 to 70. What does this indicate?

options.text: Fatigue from crying that will pass with rest
Improvement, since the heart rate is now normal
Impending arrest; start assisted ventilation
A calming effect of the oxygen being given

explanation: In children, hypoxia causes bradycardia late, just before cardiac arrest. A distressed child who becomes listless with a falling heart rate needs immediate BVM ventilation with oxygen; compressions start if the rate stays below 60 with poor perfusion.

distractorExplanations.a: Listlessness with bradycardia signals respiratory failure.
distractorExplanations.b: A falling heart rate in a hypoxic child is an ominous sign, not recovery.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen does not cause this drop; hypoxia does.

prompt: Which findings best show that an adult is in respiratory distress rather than breathing normally?

options.text: Tripod position and accessory muscle use
Rate of 16 per minute with equal chest rise
Speaking in full sentences while lying flat
SpO2 of 98% with a relaxed facial expression

explanation: Signs of respiratory distress include tripod positioning, accessory muscle use, retractions, nasal flaring, speaking in short phrases and an abnormal rate. Recognizing distress early allows oxygen or ventilation before failure.

distractorExplanations.b: That is a normal adult rate with normal chest movement.
distractorExplanations.c: Full sentences while supine suggest adequate breathing.
distractorExplanations.d: Normal saturation and a relaxed face do not suggest distress.

prompt: A tall, thin 20-year-old has sudden sharp chest pain and shortness of breath at rest. Breath sounds are diminished on the left. What should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Spontaneous pneumothorax
Pulmonary embolism from a long flight
Left-sided heart failure
Acute asthma attack

explanation: Spontaneous pneumothorax classically affects tall, thin young adults and causes sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea and diminished breath sounds on one side. EMTs give oxygen, position for comfort, watch for tension signs and transport.

distractorExplanations.b: PE usually has normal breath sounds; one-sided loss points to pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.c: Heart failure causes crackles in both bases, typically in older patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Asthma causes wheezing on both sides, not one-sided diminished sounds.

prompt: Two days after hip surgery, a patient suddenly develops shortness of breath, a heart rate of 124 and sharp chest pain. Lungs sound clear. What should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Pneumonia from immobility
Pulmonary embolism
Asthma triggered by hospital air
Anxiety about the recovery

explanation: Recent surgery and immobility raise the risk of deep vein clots that can travel to the lungs. Sudden dyspnea, tachycardia and pleuritic chest pain with clear lung sounds suggest pulmonary embolism; EMTs give oxygen and transport promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: Pneumonia develops over days with fever, cough and crackles.
distractorExplanations.c: Asthma causes wheezing, not clear lungs with sudden pleuritic pain.
distractorExplanations.d: Anxiety is a diagnosis of exclusion after serious causes are considered.

prompt: An adult choking victim becomes unresponsive. What should the EMT do next?

options.text: Do blind finger sweeps until the object is found
Keep giving abdominal thrusts with the patient lying down
Start CPR, checking the mouth before breaths
Give back blows while rolling the patient side to side

explanation: When a choking adult becomes unresponsive, lower them to the ground and start CPR; chest compressions can dislodge the object. Before each set of breaths, look in the mouth and remove any visible object. Do not perform blind finger sweeps.

distractorExplanations.a: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only what you see.
distractorExplanations.b: Once unresponsive, compressions replace abdominal thrusts.
distractorExplanations.d: Back blows are for responsive patients; unresponsive patients get CPR.

prompt: A 72-year-old diabetic woman reports unusual fatigue, nausea and shortness of breath, but no chest pain. Her skin is pale and clammy. How should the EMT treat this?

options.text: As anxiety, and advise a doctor visit tomorrow
As the flu, since there is no chest pain
As possible ACS, with prompt transport
As low blood sugar alone and give oral glucose

explanation: Atypical ACS presentations (fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, weakness) are common in women, older adults and diabetics. EMTs treat these patients as possible ACS: oxygen if hypoxic, aspirin per protocol, a 12-lead if available and prompt transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Pale, clammy skin with dyspnea is not reassuring; delay can be fatal.
distractorExplanations.b: Women, older adults and diabetics often have ACS without chest pain.
distractorExplanations.d: Check glucose, but these signs need cardiac assessment regardless.

prompt: A patient is sitting bolt upright, gasping, with crackles in both lungs and pink, frothy sputum. BP is 168/96. What is most likely?

options.text: Pneumothorax with a collapsed lung on one side
Left-sided heart failure with pulmonary edema
Asthma attack with mucus plugging the airways
Right-sided heart failure with systemic congestion

explanation: When the left ventricle fails, blood backs up into the lungs, causing crackles, severe dyspnea, orthopnea and pink, frothy sputum. EMTs keep the patient sitting up, give oxygen, consider CPAP per protocol and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Pneumothorax reduces breath sounds on one side; it does not cause crackles.
distractorExplanations.c: Asthma causes wheezing, not crackles with pink, frothy sputum.
distractorExplanations.d: Right-sided failure causes peripheral edema and JVD, not frothy sputum.

prompt: A 66-year-old with hypertension describes sudden, tearing chest pain that radiates to his back. BP is 182/100 in the right arm and 140/86 in the left. What should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Stable angina from exertion
Acute pericarditis
Musculoskeletal back strain
Aortic dissection

explanation: Sudden tearing or ripping chest pain radiating to the back, especially with a large BP difference between the arms, suggests aortic dissection. It is a surgical emergency; EMTs avoid delays, keep the patient calm and transport rapidly per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Angina is pressure relieved by rest, not tearing pain with unequal arm pressures.
distractorExplanations.b: Pericarditis causes sharp pain eased by leaning forward, not unequal BPs.
distractorExplanations.c: Strain does not cause a large BP difference between the arms.

prompt: A patient has a severe headache, confusion and vomiting with a BP of 232/134. What is the EMT's priority?

options.text: Give her own BP pills from the bottle to lower it fast
Treat the headache only and advise rest at home
Treat as a hypertensive emergency and transport
Have her lie flat and recheck the BP in an hour

explanation: Very high blood pressure with headache, confusion, vomiting or vision changes signals a hypertensive emergency that can cause stroke or seizures. EMTs monitor the airway and mental status, position for comfort and transport promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: EMTs do not give a patient's BP drugs; rapid lowering can also cause harm.
distractorExplanations.b: Headache with confusion and very high BP is an emergency.
distractorExplanations.d: Delay risks stroke, seizures and organ damage.

prompt: How deep should chest compressions be for a 6-year-old in cardiac arrest?

options.text: About 1 inch, as for a newborn
About 1.5 inches with two fingers only
One-third of chest depth, about 2 inches
At least 3 inches, deeper than for an adult

explanation: For children (1 year to puberty), compress at least one-third of the anterior-posterior chest depth, about 2 inches (5 cm), at 100–120 per minute with full recoil, using one or two hands.

distractorExplanations.a: One inch is too shallow for a child to produce blood flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Two fingers are for infants; children need one or two hands.
distractorExplanations.d: That exceeds even adult limits and risks injury.

prompt: Two EMTs are doing CPR on an infant. Which compression technique is preferred?

options.text: Two-thumb encircling hands
Two hands on the sternum as for an adult
One finger pressing on the upper sternum
Heel of one hand on the lower sternum

explanation: With two rescuers, the two-thumb encircling-hands technique gives better depth and blood flow in infants. A single rescuer may use two fingers or the heel of one hand, compressing about 1.5 inches (4 cm).

distractorExplanations.b: Adult technique is far too forceful for an infant.
distractorExplanations.c: One finger cannot produce adequate depth, and the hand position is wrong.
distractorExplanations.d: One-hand compressions are used for children, not infants.

prompt: Two EMTs are performing CPR on a 3-year-old with no advanced airway. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?

options.text: Continuous compressions with no breaths

explanation: For infants and children, two rescuers use 15 compressions to 2 breaths; a lone rescuer uses 30:2. Breaths matter because pediatric arrests are usually respiratory in origin.

distractorExplanations.a: 5:1 is an outdated ratio no longer in AHA guidelines.
distractorExplanations.c: 30:2 is used by a single rescuer for children; two rescuers use 15:2.
distractorExplanations.d: Children often arrest from respiratory causes and need breaths.

prompt: An AED is used on a 5-year-old in cardiac arrest. Which pads should the EMT apply?

options.text: Pediatric pads cut down to fit the small chest
Adult pads only, since pediatric pads are too weak
No pads, because AEDs are never used on children
Pediatric pads, or adult pads if none

explanation: Children under 8 years should get pediatric pads or a dose attenuator. If none is available, adult pads are used, placed front and back if they would otherwise touch. Defibrillation should not be delayed.

distractorExplanations.a: Pads are never cut; anterior-posterior placement fixes size problems.
distractorExplanations.b: Pediatric pads or attenuators reduce the dose for small children.
distractorExplanations.c: AEDs are used on children; pediatric equipment is preferred.

prompt: Two EMTs are doing CPR on an adult. How often should they switch compressors?

options.text: Every 30 seconds to keep compressions fast
Never, so one person keeps a steady rhythm
About every 2 minutes, at the rhythm check
Only when the compressor says they are tired

explanation: Compression quality drops after about 2 minutes even when rescuers feel fine. Switching at each 2-minute rhythm analysis, in under 5 seconds, keeps depth and rate high while limiting pauses.

distractorExplanations.a: Very frequent switches add pauses and reduce compression time.
distractorExplanations.b: Compression quality declines after about 2 minutes.
distractorExplanations.d: Fatigue reduces quality before rescuers notice it.

prompt: How long should an EMT take to check for a pulse in an unresponsive adult before starting CPR?

options.text: About 30 seconds at the carotid
At least 15 seconds to be certain
A full minute while counting the rate
No more than 10 seconds

explanation: Pulse checks, done at the same time as checking breathing, take no more than 10 seconds. If a definite pulse is not felt, start compressions immediately.

distractorExplanations.a: Thirty seconds wastes time when the brain needs blood flow.
distractorExplanations.b: Longer checks delay compressions; if unsure, start CPR.
distractorExplanations.c: A minute-long check would cost critical perfusion time.

prompt: An adult in cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of rainwater. What should the EMT do before applying AED pads?

options.text: Move him out of the water and dry the chest
Pour more water on the chest to improve contact
Apply the pads over the wet skin to save time
Skip the AED because water makes shocking unsafe

explanation: Water conducts electricity across the skin, which reduces the shock delivered to the heart and can endanger rescuers. Move the patient out of standing water, quickly dry the chest and then apply the pads. Small puddles under the patient are less of a concern than a wet chest.

distractorExplanations.b: Water spreads the current across the skin instead of through the heart.
distractorExplanations.c: Water conducts current and lowers shock effectiveness.
distractorExplanations.d: The AED is still used after moving the patient and drying the chest.

prompt: An unresponsive patient has a pacemaker bump under the skin below the right collarbone. Where should the AED pad go?

options.text: Skip the AED, since the pacemaker will act
On the left side only, with no second pad
Directly over the device for a better reading
At least 1 inch away from the device

explanation: Implanted pacemakers and defibrillators are usually below the collarbone. Place the pad at least 1 inch away (or use anterior-posterior placement) so the device does not block the shock. Do not delay defibrillation.

distractorExplanations.a: A pacemaker cannot treat VF; the AED is still needed.
distractorExplanations.b: Two pads are always needed to send current through the heart.
distractorExplanations.c: Shocking through the device can damage it and weaken the shock.

prompt: A patient in cardiac arrest has a nitroglycerin patch where an AED pad should go. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Move the pad to the abdomen instead
Skip that pad and use only the other one
Remove the patch with gloves, wipe skin
Put the pad directly over the patch

explanation: Medication patches can block current and cause skin burns under an AED pad. With gloved hands, remove the patch and wipe the skin before placing the pad. Gloves protect the rescuer from absorbing the drug.

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal placement does not send current through the heart.
distractorExplanations.b: Both pads are needed for the shock to cross the heart.
distractorExplanations.d: The patch can block current and cause burns.

prompt: Which feature suggests a myocardial infarction rather than stable angina?

options.text: Pain fully relieved by a single nitroglycerin dose
Pain that is familiar and follows the usual pattern
Pain that starts with exertion and stops with rest in minutes
Pain lasting over 30 minutes despite rest and nitroglycerin

explanation: Stable angina is chest discomfort triggered by exertion and relieved within minutes by rest or nitroglycerin. Pain that lasts longer than about 30 minutes, occurs at rest or is not relieved suggests myocardial infarction and needs emergency care.

distractorExplanations.a: Prompt relief with nitroglycerin fits angina more than MI.
distractorExplanations.b: A stable, familiar pattern suggests angina, not a new MI.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the typical pattern of stable angina.

prompt: A man found with drug paraphernalia is pulseless and apneic. What is the EMT's first priority?

options.text: Place him in the recovery position and give naloxone
Start CPR; naloxone does not replace it
Give rescue breaths only, since it is an overdose
Give naloxone and wait for it to restart the heart

explanation: In opioid-associated cardiac arrest, standard CPR and the AED come first. Naloxone may be given per protocol, but it does not restart the heart and must not delay compressions or defibrillation.

distractorExplanations.a: The recovery position is for patients with a pulse who are breathing.
distractorExplanations.c: A pulseless patient needs compressions, not breaths alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Naloxone reverses breathing depression; it cannot restore a pulse.

prompt: An EMT is applying a tourniquet for massive bleeding from the forearm. Where should it be placed?

options.text: Below the wound to stop blood returning
Directly over the wound to compress the vessel
2–3 inches above the wound, not over a joint
Over the elbow joint so it holds securely

explanation: A tourniquet goes 2–3 inches above the wound (or high and tight if the site is unclear), never over a joint. It is tightened until bleeding stops and the distal pulse is gone, and the time is noted. A second tourniquet can be placed above the first if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: A tourniquet below the wound does not stop arterial inflow.
distractorExplanations.b: Over the wound, the tourniquet cannot compress the vessel above the injury.
distractorExplanations.d: Joints prevent the tourniquet from compressing the artery.

prompt: A stab wound in the groin is bleeding heavily. A tourniquet cannot be applied there. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Place a tourniquet on the thigh below the wound
Elevate the leg and wait for the bleeding to slow
Apply a loose dressing and transport without pressure
Pack the wound with gauze and hold firm pressure

explanation: Junctional wounds (groin, armpit, neck) cannot take a tourniquet. Pack the wound tightly with hemostatic or plain gauze, then hold firm direct pressure for several minutes per protocol, and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.a: A tourniquet below the wound does not stop flow from above.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevation alone does not stop junctional arterial bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: A loose dressing does not control heavy bleeding.

prompt: After a diving injury, a patient cannot move his legs. BP is 82/50, pulse 54, and his skin is warm and dry. What type of shock is this?

options.text: Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Anaphylactic shock
Neurogenic shock

explanation: Spinal cord injury can disrupt sympathetic control, causing vasodilation with low BP, a normal or slow pulse and warm, dry skin below the injury. EMTs maintain spinal motion restriction, support ABCs, keep the patient warm and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Hypovolemic shock causes a fast pulse and cool, clammy skin.
distractorExplanations.b: Cardiogenic shock usually shows cool, clammy skin and signs of heart failure.
distractorExplanations.c: Anaphylaxis brings hives and wheezing, not paralysis after a dive.

prompt: A worker has a partial-thickness burn on the forearm from hot oil, just now. What is the first step in burn care?

options.text: Pop the blisters so the burn can drain
Pack the arm in ice to stop the pain fast
Stop the burning and cool with clean water
Apply butter or ointment to seal in moisture

explanation: Stop the burning process first, then cool small burns with clean, cool (not ice-cold) water for several minutes per protocol. Remove jewelry, cover with a dry sterile dressing and prevent hypothermia in large burns. Never use ice or ointments.

distractorExplanations.a: Intact blisters protect against infection and should be left alone.
distractorExplanations.b: Ice causes further tissue damage and hypothermia.
distractorExplanations.d: Greasy substances trap heat and contaminate the wound.

prompt: A farmer has dry lime powder on his arms and chest. What should the EMT do first?

options.text: Brush off the dry powder, then flush with water
Neutralize it with vinegar from the farmhouse
Cover the area with a wet dressing for transport
Flush immediately with a small amount of water

explanation: Dry chemicals such as lime are brushed off first, with PPE, because water can react with them. After brushing, flush with large amounts of water for a prolonged period. Neutralizing agents are not used.

distractorExplanations.b: Neutralizers create heat and further injure the skin.
distractorExplanations.c: A wet dressing reacts with the lime left on the skin.
distractorExplanations.d: A small amount of water can activate the lime and worsen the burn.

prompt: A worker touched a high-voltage line. He has a small burn on the hand and another on the foot. He is alert. Why does he still need transport?

options.text: He might be carrying a residual electric charge
Internal injury and dysrhythmias may be hidden
Electrical burns are always full-thickness
The small burns will need stitches tonight

explanation: Electrical injury travels between entry and exit points and can damage muscle, nerves and the heart well beyond the visible burns. Patients may develop dysrhythmias or cardiac arrest, so they need monitoring and transport even if they look well.

distractorExplanations.a: Patients do not hold a charge once the source is off.
distractorExplanations.c: Burn depth varies; hidden internal damage is the main concern.
distractorExplanations.d: Small surface burns rarely need sutures; the concern is internal.

prompt: A man rescued from a house fire has soot around his mouth, singed nose hairs and a hoarse voice. What is the EMT's main concern?

options.text: Airway swelling that can obstruct
Eye irritation from the smoke
Dehydration from the heat of the fire
Burns to the skin of his face only

explanation: Soot in the mouth, singed nasal hair, facial burns and hoarseness suggest inhalation injury. The airway can swell and close within minutes to hours. EMTs give high-flow oxygen, monitor closely, request ALS and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.b: Eye irritation is minor compared with airway swelling.
distractorExplanations.c: Fluid loss is a later concern; the airway is the immediate threat.
distractorExplanations.d: Facial burns matter, but airway burns can close the airway.

prompt: Using the rule of nines, an adult has burns over the front and back of the entire right arm and the whole front of the trunk. What is the estimated total body surface area burned?
explanation: In the adult rule of nines, each whole arm is 9% and the front of the trunk is 18%. 9% + 18% = 27% TBSA. The palm method (about 1% per patient palm) helps estimate scattered burns.

distractorExplanations.a: 18% is only the front of the trunk; the arm adds 9%.
distractorExplanations.c: 36% counts the entire trunk (front and back), which is not burned.
distractorExplanations.d: 45% counts both arms and the full trunk, which overestimates.

prompt: After a high-speed crash, an adult has a GCS of 12, BP 84/50 and respirations of 32. Where should the EMT transport, if one is reachable?

options.text: The patient's primary care doctor's office
The highest-level trauma center in the area
The closest hospital regardless of capability
The nearest community clinic for stabilization

explanation: Field trauma triage guidelines send patients with altered mental status, systolic BP under 90 or abnormal respirations after significant trauma to the highest-level trauma center available. Early notification speeds surgical care.

distractorExplanations.a: An office cannot manage life-threatening injuries.
distractorExplanations.c: Field triage guidelines direct these patients to trauma centers.
distractorExplanations.d: Clinics cannot provide surgical trauma care.

prompt: An EMT is splinting a suspected midshaft forearm fracture. Which principle applies?

options.text: Splint only the fracture site, leaving the joints free
Skip pulse checks to avoid moving the arm
Straighten every deformity before splinting
Immobilize the joints above and below, and check PMS

explanation: Long-bone fractures are splinted so the joints above and below are immobilized. Pulse, motor function and sensation are checked before and after splinting; loss of PMS after splinting means the splint must be adjusted.

distractorExplanations.a: Movement at the joints moves the fracture ends.
distractorExplanations.b: PMS is checked before and after splinting to catch compromise.
distractorExplanations.c: Long-bone shafts may be gently realigned per protocol; joints are splinted as found.

prompt: A worker has a metal rod impaled in his right eye. What is the correct care?

options.text: Cover only the injured eye to let him see
Flush the eye with water around the rod
Stabilize the rod and cover both eyes
Remove the rod gently and patch the eye

explanation: Impaled objects in the eye are stabilized in place, often with a cup over the object, and both eyes are covered because the eyes move together. The patient is kept calm and transported.

distractorExplanations.a: Moving the uninjured eye moves the injured one too.
distractorExplanations.b: Flushing is for chemical exposure, not impaled objects.
distractorExplanations.d: Removal can cause more damage and loss of eye contents.

prompt: An adult has a persistent nosebleed after being struck in the face. There is no suspected spinal injury. How should the EMT position the patient?

options.text: Standing with the head tilted far back
Supine with the legs raised high
Lying flat with the head tilted back on a pillow
Sitting, leaning forward, nostrils pinched

explanation: For epistaxis without spinal concerns, have the patient sit and lean forward while pinching the soft part of the nostrils firmly. This lets blood drain out rather than down the throat, reducing vomiting and aspiration risk.

distractorExplanations.a: Blood flows down the throat and may be aspirated.
distractorExplanations.b: Raising the legs does not control a nosebleed.
distractorExplanations.c: Tilting back makes blood run down the throat and causes vomiting.

prompt: A motorcyclist wearing a full-face helmet is breathing adequately, and the helmet fits snugly. When should the EMT remove it?

options.text: Only if it blocks airway care or does not fit
Never, even in cardiac arrest
Always, as soon as the patient is reached
Only after the patient is placed on a long board

explanation: A snug helmet that does not interfere with airway management or assessment is left on and stabilized. It is removed if it blocks airway or ventilation, if it is loose, or if the patient needs CPR, using a two-rescuer technique.

distractorExplanations.b: A helmet that prevents CPR or airway care must come off.
distractorExplanations.c: Unnecessary removal moves the cervical spine.
distractorExplanations.d: Removal decisions depend on airway access, not board placement.

prompt: An unrestrained driver hit the dashboard with his knees in a frontal crash. Which injury pattern should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Wrist and forearm fractures only
Knee, femur and hip injuries
Neck injury from a rear impact
Isolated ankle fracture only

explanation: In a frontal crash with a down-and-under path, the knees strike the dashboard and force travels up the femur to the hip, causing knee, femur and posterior hip dislocation or fracture.

distractorExplanations.a: The knee-dashboard impact transmits force up the leg, not the arms.
distractorExplanations.c: This is a frontal crash with a down-and-under path, not a rear impact.
distractorExplanations.d: The force travels upward from the knee, not down to the ankle.

prompt: A woman 32 weeks pregnant is secured supine for spinal motion restriction after a crash. She becomes dizzy and hypotensive. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Tilt the board or move the uterus left
Give her water to raise the blood pressure
Sit her upright, removing spinal precautions
Raise the legs and keep her flat on the back

explanation: After about 20 weeks, the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the patient lies flat, reducing blood return to the heart (supine hypotensive syndrome). Tilt the whole board about 15–30 degrees to the left or manually displace the uterus to the left.

distractorExplanations.b: Oral fluids do not fix vena cava compression.
distractorExplanations.c: Tilting the board keeps spinal precautions while relieving pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: The uterus is still compressing the vena cava while supine.

prompt: Using the Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale, which three things does the EMT check?

options.text: Blood pressure, pulse and breathing rate
Facial droop, arm drift and speech
Gait, vision and headache severity
Pupils, grip strength and blood sugar

explanation: The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale checks facial droop (smile), arm drift (arms held out with eyes closed) and speech (repeat a sentence). Any abnormal finding suggests stroke; EMTs also note the time last known well and check glucose.

distractorExplanations.a: Vital signs are important but are not the stroke scale.
distractorExplanations.c: These may be stroke signs but are not the Cincinnati items.
distractorExplanations.d: Glucose is checked separately; these are not the scale's items.

prompt: A man woke up at 0700 with weakness on one side. He was last seen normal going to bed at 2300. What time should the EMT report as last known well?

options.text: Midnight, as a standard estimate
The time EMS arrived on scene
0700, when he woke with symptoms
2300, when last seen normal

explanation: Stroke treatment windows are based on the last time the patient was known to be normal. For a patient who wakes up with symptoms, that is the time they went to sleep normal, not the time they woke up.

distractorExplanations.a: Guessing a standard time can make him wrongly eligible for treatment.
distractorExplanations.b: EMS arrival time has no bearing on stroke onset.
distractorExplanations.c: Symptoms were discovered at waking; onset could be any time overnight.

prompt: A type 1 diabetic has fruity breath, deep rapid respirations, and has been vomiting for two days. Her glucose meter reads 'HI.' What does this suggest?

options.text: Hyperventilation from anxiety about her illness
Alcohol intoxication from the smell of her breath
Hypoglycemia needing oral glucose right away
Diabetic ketoacidosis from very high blood sugar

explanation: Diabetic ketoacidosis causes very high glucose, dehydration, vomiting, fruity (ketone) breath and deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations. EMTs support ABCs, do not give sugar and transport promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: Kussmaul breathing compensates for acidosis; it is not anxiety.
distractorExplanations.b: Fruity breath here comes from ketones, not alcohol.
distractorExplanations.c: A 'HI' reading means very high, not low, blood sugar.

prompt: A hypothermic patient found outdoors is shivering, confused and has a weak pulse. How should the EMT move him?

options.text: Rub his arms and legs firmly to warm them
Gently, keeping him horizontal
Sit him upright and give hot coffee
Have him walk to the ambulance to warm up

explanation: A cold heart is irritable, and rough handling can trigger ventricular fibrillation. Move hypothermic patients gently and horizontally, remove wet clothing, insulate them, start passive and active external rewarming per protocol and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Rubbing can push cold blood to the core and injure tissue.
distractorExplanations.c: Caffeine and an upright posture can worsen instability.
distractorExplanations.d: Exertion can trigger dangerous heart rhythms in a cold heart.

prompt: A hiker has frostbite on both feet and is 2 hours from the trailhead. What should the EMT avoid?

options.text: Removing wet socks and covering the feet loosely
Thawing the feet if they may refreeze
Keeping the patient warm during transport
Padding between the toes with dry gauze

explanation: Thawing and refreezing causes more tissue damage than delayed thawing. Frostbitten areas are protected, not rubbed or rewarmed in the field when refreezing is possible. Wet clothing is removed and digits are padded with dry dressings.

distractorExplanations.a: Removing wet clothing and protecting the feet is appropriate.
distractorExplanations.c: Overall warming helps prevent worsening hypothermia.
distractorExplanations.d: Dry, loose padding between digits is appropriate.

prompt: Police have restrained a combative, agitated patient. How should the EMT position him for transport?

options.text: Face down with an officer kneeling on his back
Sitting upright and alone in the back of the unit
Supine or on his side, monitored closely
Face down with hands and feet tied together

explanation: Restrained patients are transported supine or on their side, never face down or hog-tied, and are continuously monitored for airway, breathing and circulation. Agitated delirium can lead to sudden cardiac arrest.

distractorExplanations.a: Weight on the back restricts breathing and can be fatal.
distractorExplanations.b: An agitated patient must always be monitored.
distractorExplanations.d: Prone hobble restraint can cause positional asphyxia and death.

prompt: A 3-year-old may have swallowed some of grandma's pills 20 minutes ago. She is alert. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Watch at home for an hour before deciding
Make her vomit by putting a finger down her throat
Bring the pill bottle; call poison control
Give milk so the pills will dissolve harmlessly

explanation: For possible ingestions, EMTs gather the container, estimate time and amount, contact poison control or medical direction and transport. Induced vomiting is not recommended, and activated charcoal is given only per protocol to alert patients who can swallow.

distractorExplanations.a: Some drugs cause delayed toxicity; the child needs assessment.
distractorExplanations.b: Induced vomiting is not recommended and risks aspiration.
distractorExplanations.d: Milk does not neutralize most drugs and can delay care.

prompt: A 74-year-old man with severe low back pain is pale and diaphoretic. BP is 82/50, and a pulsating mass is felt in his abdomen. What should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Constipation causing abdominal distension
Kidney stones causing severe flank pain
Muscle strain from lifting heavy boxes
A leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm

explanation: A pulsating abdominal mass with back or abdominal pain and signs of shock in an older adult suggests a leaking abdominal aortic aneurysm. EMTs palpate gently, treat for shock and transport rapidly to a surgical center.

distractorExplanations.a: Constipation does not cause shock or a pulsatile mass.
distractorExplanations.b: Kidney stones do not cause a pulsating mass with shock.
distractorExplanations.c: Strain does not cause hypotension and a pulsatile mass.

prompt: A 26-year-old woman has sudden severe lower abdominal pain, a missed period and dizziness. Her pulse is 128 and BP 88/56. What should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Appendicitis without bleeding
Urinary tract infection
Normal menstrual cramps
Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

explanation: A woman of childbearing age with abdominal pain, a missed period and signs of shock should be treated as having a ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise. EMTs treat for shock and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.a: Appendicitis rarely causes this degree of shock early.
distractorExplanations.b: A UTI does not cause shock with a missed period.
distractorExplanations.c: Cramps do not cause tachycardia and hypotension.

prompt: A newborn delivered in the field is limp. After drying and stimulating, the heart rate is 80 per minute with weak breathing. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Give blow-by oxygen only and observe
Begin BVM ventilation with room air
Start chest compressions immediately
Keep rubbing the back and wait 5 minutes

explanation: If a newborn's heart rate is below 100 or breathing is inadequate after drying and stimulation, start positive-pressure ventilation at 40–60 breaths per minute, usually with room air for term babies. If the rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation, start compressions.

distractorExplanations.a: A heart rate under 100 with weak breathing needs ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions start only if the rate stays below 60 despite ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting delays ventilation in a newborn whose rate is under 100.

prompt: After starting care for a patient, an EMT leaves her with a bystander to go to another call. What legal problem is this?

options.text: Abandonment
Assault
Negligence
Breach of confidentiality

explanation: Abandonment is ending care without transferring the patient to someone of equal or higher training. Once care begins, the EMT must continue until a qualified provider takes over or the patient refuses.

distractorExplanations.b: Assault is threatening to harm or treat someone without consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Negligence needs a duty, a breach, damages and causation; leaving care is specifically abandonment.
distractorExplanations.d: Confidentiality concerns sharing patient information.

prompt: When medical direction gives an EMT a medication order by radio, what should the EMT do?

options.text: Repeat the order back word for word
Write it down later after the call ends
Change the dose if it seems too high
Give the drug immediately without repeating

explanation: Closed-loop communication means repeating an order back exactly, waiting for confirmation and then carrying it out. If an order seems wrong, the EMT questions it with medical direction before acting.

distractorExplanations.b: Orders are confirmed and documented at the time.
distractorExplanations.c: Concerns are raised with the physician; the EMT does not change the dose alone.
distractorExplanations.d: Without read-back, misheard orders can lead to errors.

prompt: EMTs arrive at a tanker rollover with a leaking unknown substance. Where should they stage?

options.text: Downwind to smell for leaks
As close as possible to treat patients fast
Uphill and upwind at a safe distance
Downhill so runoff can be seen

explanation: At hazmat scenes, EMTs stage uphill and upwind, identify the substance from a safe distance (placards, Emergency Response Guidebook) and wait for hazmat teams. Patients are treated after decontamination.

distractorExplanations.a: Downwind positions put responders directly in the vapor cloud.
distractorExplanations.b: Untrained responders entering the hot zone become victims.
distractorExplanations.d: Liquids and heavy vapors flow downhill toward responders.

prompt: A woman 36 weeks pregnant with a severe headache and swelling has a seizure. What condition should the EMT suspect?

options.text: Epilepsy unrelated to pregnancy
Supine hypotensive syndrome
Hypoglycemia from skipped meals
Eclampsia

explanation: Preeclampsia (high BP, headache, swelling, vision changes) can progress to eclampsia with seizures after 20 weeks of pregnancy. EMTs protect the airway, place the patient on her left side, give oxygen and transport rapidly to an obstetric facility.

distractorExplanations.a: A first seizure late in pregnancy with these signs suggests eclampsia.
distractorExplanations.b: Supine hypotension causes dizziness, not seizures with headache.
distractorExplanations.c: Check glucose, but headache, swelling and seizure point to eclampsia.

prompt: Ten minutes after a field delivery and placenta delivery, the mother is bleeding heavily and her uterus feels soft and boggy. What should the EMT do?

options.text: Have her stand up to help the blood drain
Pack gauze into the vagina to stop the bleeding
Massage the uterus firmly and treat for shock
Wait 30 minutes to see if the bleeding slows

explanation: A soft, boggy uterus after delivery means it is not contracting (uterine atony), the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage. EMTs massage the fundus firmly, encourage breastfeeding if possible, treat for shock and transport promptly. More than 500 mL of blood loss is significant.

distractorExplanations.a: Standing worsens hypotension from blood loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Nothing is inserted into the vagina; external pressure and fundal massage are used.
distractorExplanations.d: Postpartum hemorrhage can become life-threatening within minutes.
